chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah al-Ansari, and lice were falling from his head, so he said, 'Do the insects of your head afflict you?' He said, 'Yes.'
So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [from shaving] must offer a ransom of fasting [three days] or charity or a sacrifice.

So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ordered him, and he shaved his head, and made upon him fasting for three days, and charity to six poor people, for each poor person two muds, and the sacrifice is one sheep.

key_terms.إِحْرَام: Sacred state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.صَدَقَة: Charity, specifically feeding the poor in this context
key_terms.فِدْيَة: Ransom or compensation offered in lieu of an act
key_terms.كَفَّارَة: Expiation or ransom for a religious obligation or breach

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for shaving hair in Ihram due to lice or illness, and is it mandatory to perform all three options?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* links the specific ruling for lice-induced hair cutting to the broader legal framework of *kaffarah* in Surah Al-Baqarah, illustrating the Prophet's practical application of the verse to Ka'b ibn Ujrah. It establishes a critical Shia jurisprudential principle: the conjunction 'aw' (or) in the Quranic text grants the individual the choice (*ikhtiyar*) among the three expiation methods, provided they can afford them. This hadith serves as a primary evidence for the flexibility in fulfilling religious duties when the primary obligation is interrupted by necessity or error.
